nameStory: The name 'devil's walkingstick' comes from this plant's absolutely wicked spines that cover nearly every surface - stems, leaf stalks, and even the midribs of leaves! Early settlers thought it looked like a walking stick that only the devil himself would dare to use. The alternative name 'Hercules' club' suggests you'd need superhuman strength to wield such a thorny staff.
description: Devil's walkingstick is a small tree or large shrub that looks almost tropical with its enormous, lacy compound leaves. It can grow 10-25 feet tall with a slender, usually unbranched trunk that's absolutely covered in sharp spines. The whole plant has an exotic, almost prehistoric appearance that makes it stand out dramatically in New England's forests. Despite its fearsome armament of thorns, it's actually in the same family as English ivy.

idTips.label: Spines
idTips.description: Vicious, sharp spines cover almost every surface - the trunk, branches, leaf stalks, and even the leaf midribs. These aren't just prickles but substantial thorns that can easily puncture skin and clothing.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Enormous compound leaves can be 2-4 feet long, divided and subdivided into many small leaflets that create a delicate, lacy appearance. The leaves emerge from the top of the trunk in a palm-like cluster.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Usually grows as a single, slender, unbranched trunk topped with a cluster of huge leaves, giving it an almost palm tree-like silhouette that's unique in New England forests.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small white flowers appear in large, branched clusters above the leaves in late summer, creating a frothy, cream-colored display that can be 12-18 inches across.

idTips.label: Fruit
idTips.description: Small dark purple berries ripen in fall, arranged in the same large branched clusters as the flowers. Birds love them, which helps spread the seeds.

habitat: Devil's walkingstick prefers rich, moist woodland soils and forest edges throughout New England, though it's quite rare in our region. You're most likely to spot it in protected valleys, along streams, or in areas where the soil stays consistently moist. It often appears in disturbed forest areas and can tolerate both sun and partial shade.

seasonality.spring: New leaves emerge late in spring, unfurling from large buds at the top of the spiny trunk. The compound leaves start small but rapidly expand to their full impressive size.
seasonality.summer: The plant reaches peak leafiness and produces its showy white flower clusters in late summer. This is when it's most tropical-looking and easiest to spot.
seasonality.fall: Dark purple berries ripen and leaves turn yellow before dropping. The bare, spiny trunk becomes very obvious once the leaves fall.
seasonality.winter: Leafless but unmistakable due to the spiny trunk and distinctive palm-like branching pattern at the top. Large leaf scars mark where the huge compound leaves were attached.

funFact: This plant is so rare in New England that it's been spotted only once in our region according to naturalist databases, making it one of the most elusive native plants you could possibly encounter on a nature walk!
confusionNotes: Devil's walkingstick shares the common names 'Hercules' club' and 'prickly ash' with the completely unrelated toothache tree (Zanthoxylum clava-herculis), which can cause real confusion. The key difference: toothache tree has much smaller, regularly compound leaves and different spine patterns, while devil's walkingstick has those enormous, doubly-compound lacy leaves.
contextualKnowledge: Don't be fooled by the shared common names - this plant has no medicinal properties like the true toothache tree it's often confused with. Despite its tropical appearance, devil's walkingstick is completely hardy in New England and is actually native to eastern North America, not some exotic import.
compareHints: Among its Aralia relatives in New England, devil's walkingstick is unmistakable due to its woody, tree-like growth and extensive spines. Wild sarsaparilla stays low and herbaceous, American spikenard is a bushy herb, and bristly sarsaparilla, while having some prickles, is much smaller and shrubby. Only devil's walkingstick combines the tree-like stature with the fearsome armament of spines covering nearly every surface.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Wild sarsaparilla is much shorter than its Aralia relatives - bristly sarsaparilla grows taller with prickly stems, while American spikenard can reach 6 feet with multiple compound leaves and a more robust appearance.

Among New England's Aralia species, bristly sarsaparilla is the shortest and most rough-textured, preferring dry soils unlike wild sarsaparilla's forest preference or American spikenard's love of rich, moist areas.

American spikenard is much larger and more robust than its relatives - wild sarsaparilla stays close to the ground with leaves only 6-12 inches tall, while bristly sarsaparilla is covered in prickles.

Among its Aralia relatives in New England, Japanese angelica tree is by far the tallest and most tree-like, while wild sarsaparilla stays low to the ground and American spikenard is an herbaceous perennial.
Unlike its native New England Aralia cousins which are mostly low woodland herbs, Chinese angelica-tree grows much larger and lacks the thorns found on devil's walkingstick.
Japanese spikenard dwarfs its New England relatives like wild sarsaparilla and American spikenard, growing 2-3 times taller with much more robust stems.
